opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it really came down to scale and the kind of problems you could work on there. I'd been fascinated for a long time by the idea that if you could get a machine to genuinely understand language, to read text and answer questions about it, reason over it, you'd unlock a huge amount of what we think of as intelligence. So much human knowledge is written down, and text is the interface we use to communicate with each other. Teaching machines to learn from that felt like one of the most important problems out there.

Google was a unique place to pursue that. You had an enormous amount of real-world text data, serious compute, and some of the best people in the field all sitting close together. And the problems weren't just academic. Things like search and question answering directly touch billions of people, so you got this tight loop between research ideas and real use cases. If something worked, you could see very quickly whether it mattered.

The culture was also very open and collaborative. You could walk over to someone working on translation or on a completely different modeling approach and just start talking through ideas. A lot of the most interesting work came out of that kind of cross-pollination, people from different backgrounds asking whether there was a simpler, more parallel way to model language than the recurrent approaches everyone was using at the time.

So it was really that combination: an important problem, the resources to attack it seriously, and a group of people who were willing to try fairly radical ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says he wanted machines to learn from text and understand language, but it does not mention the cat neuron paper or frame his goal as a text analogue of its demonstrated learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I came to Google by a bit of a roundabout path. I'm originally from Ukraine, and I was doing a lot of competitive programming and working on startups before I joined. What drew me in was that, at the time, Google was really one of the only places where you had all three ingredients together: enormous amounts of text data, the compute to actually train large models on it, and a research culture that let you take a swing at hard, somewhat unformed problems.

I ended up on the research side working on question answering, and that problem in particular was fascinating to me. You give a machine a document and a question, and it has to actually read and reason about the text to produce an answer. It's not just classification or ranking, it's something closer to understanding. And in a production setting, you couldn't cheat. Things had to work at scale, and they had to be fast enough to actually serve. So you were constantly forced to confront what was really going on in the models rather than just chasing a benchmark.

That's also the environment where the frustrations with recurrent networks started to build up. Training them on long sequences was slow, they were hard to parallelize, and it felt like we were fighting the architecture instead of the problem. Being surrounded by people like Ashish, Noam, Jakob, and Lukasz, who were thinking about the same bottlenecks from different angles, is really what made the Transformer work possible. It was less that I chose Google for a specific reason and more that it was the place where the right people and the right constraints happened to collide.

r001.rationale: The response says Google appealed because of its text data, compute, and research culture, and describes work on question answering. It does not state that Illia joined Google Research to pursue a text analogue of learning demonstrated in the cat neuron paper.

astra-6.text: What appealed to me was the chance to work on language understanding at a scale where it could be useful to people. Google had the research expertise, the computing resources, and real problems in search where understanding text mattered. You could explore how a model learns what a question means, how it finds relevant information, and how it might produce an answer. That connection between fundamental research and practical applications was very exciting to me.

sol-6.1.text: What appealed to me was the opportunity to work on language understanding at a scale where it could be useful. Google had both the research environment and products like Search, where understanding what somebody means is a very practical problem. You’re not just matching words—you want a machine to connect a question to information that answers it, even if the wording is completely different. That connection between a fundamental research problem and a real application was very exciting to me.
